title: MDMA-Assisted Couple Psychotherapy for PTSD in First Responders: A Phase I Feasibility Study (PACT-MDMA)
official: Evaluating the Safety, Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of Process-Centred MDMA-Assisted Couple Psychotherapy (PACT-MDMA) for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in First Responders
summary:
This study is the first step of a research programme on a new treatment for first responders with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): couple therapy in which both partners take MDMA, under medical supervision, in three of fourteen sessions. The treatment is called Process-Centred MDMA-Assisted Couple Psychotherapy, or PACT-MDMA.

Current treatments help many people with PTSD, but many drop out or improve only in part, and few treatments work directly on the relationship, which PTSD strains and which can help recovery. MDMA-assisted therapy has been tested in large trials in the United States, but these studies' designs have been criticised, and the therapy component of the treatment has rarely been specified or measured. No Canadian study has tested MDMA-assisted therapy in first responders, and none has tested it with couples.

This feasibility study at the University of Ottawa will enrol six to ten couples in which one partner is a current or former first responder with PTSD. It asks whether the treatment can be delivered safely, whether couples can be recruited and kept in the study, and whether the sessions and measures work as planned. It does not aim to prove that the treatment works. Two exploratory hypotheses will be examined: that the partner with PTSD will show a reduction in clinician-rated PTSD severity from baseline to the end of treatment that is maintained six months later, and that the other partner will accommodate PTSD symptoms less while both partners report a better relationship over the same period.

A nurse is present and a physician on call during every MDMA session; all sessions are recorded so that the therapy can be checked for fidelity to its written principles; and the research, therapy and medical roles are kept separate. If this phase succeeds, a second phase would compare PACT-MDMA with standard PTSD therapy in about 24 couples in Ottawa and Montreal, and a third would extend the study to several Canadian sites.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria (both partners unless stated):

* Aged 18 years or older
* One partner (the index participant) is a current or former first responder with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder or complex post-traumatic stress disorder
* In a relationship of at least 12 months and currently cohabiting
* Fluent in French or English (reading, writing and speaking)
* Willing to attend the therapy in person at the study site and to have all sessions audio- and video-recorded
* Able to name a supportive person not participating in the study as emergency contact
* Willing and able to provide informed consent and to take part in all study procedures
* The study is inclusive of all gender identities, sexual orientations, cultural backgrounds and religious affiliations

Exclusion Criteria (both partners, since both receive MDMA):

* Current diagnosis of a substance use disorder (moderate to severe)
* Current use of contraindicated psychoactive medications (e.g., SSRIs, MAOIs), herbal supplements, or prescription or non-prescription medications that cannot be safely tapered before the study
* Current or previous use of MDMA or other psychedelics
* Uncontrolled hypertension, significant cardiovascular disease, or another medical condition contraindicating MDMA
* Pregnancy or breastfeeding
* Current participation in another clinical trial
* History of psychotic disorder or of a disorder with psychotic features, bipolar I disorder, or borderline personality disorder
* Active suicidal ideation, recent suicide attempt, or danger to others
* Cognitive impairment that limits the ability to provide informed consent or to take part in therapy
* Current conventional or PTSD-focused psychotherapy, or another procedure likely to affect study outcomes (e.g., other psychedelic-assisted therapy, electroconvulsive therapy, transcranial magnetic stimulation)
* Relational ambivalence, including current plans to separate or divorce
* High-conflict relationship including physical violence

Final medical eligibility rests with the Medical Director, who may exclude on clinical judgement even where formal criteria are met.
